author: Ivy Secrest
title: Chief deputy receives national award for innovative mental health system - NewsBreak
text:
By Ivy Secrest ,
8 hours ago
CHEYENNE — The National Sheriffs’ Association has awarded Laramie County Sheriff’s Office Chief Deputy Perry Rockvam its Corrections/Jail Innovations of the Year Award, honoring efforts to modernize how mental health is addressed in the jail.
The national award recognizes outstanding leadership, innovation and exceptional contributions to correctional facility management and humane practices.
In Rockvam’s case, those qualities were apparent through his “visionary leadership” in developing and sustaining Wyoming’s first comprehensive Special Management Housing Unit, according to a press release sent by LCSO. The unit is dedicated entirely to inmates experiencing serious mental illness and complex medical needs.
“I very much appreciate the nomination,” Rockvam said. “It’s just very kind, because, I just look at it as just doing what I’m supposed to be doing.”
Coming into the job, Rockvam said Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak made it clear to him and his staff that the jail needed to improve how those experiencing mental illness were handled.
Several inmates come into the jail while in active crisis, often posing a danger to themselves or others. The expectation is that these inmates be housed at the jail until a bed at the State Hospital opens up, Rockvam said, but that sometimes takes up to a year, during which inmates’ mental health regresses.
“This is an issue that all jails are dealing with in our society today,” Rockvam said.
So, Rockvam began traveling to other jails to look for solutions, which eventually led to the construction of the Special Management Housing Unit and mental health pods.
With input from qualified mental health professionals and insights from nearby facilities, such as the Boulder County Jail in Colorado, Rockvam successfully repurposed the jail’s 1980s-era infrastructure into a modern, therapeutic environment.
The upgrades included:
Psychiatric-grade furniture to maximize safety.Expanded camera coverage for enhanced observation and security.Calming murals specifically designed to reduce environmental stress and support inmate emotional regulation.Reutilizing existing space was a fiscally responsible way to achieve this goal, Kozak said.
“Chief Deputy Rockvam’s forward-thinking leadership reflects our agency’s deep commitment to safety, fiscal responsibility and humane correctional practices,” Kozak said. “His work has not only improved safety within our facility but has also drawn national attention as a model for agencies across the country.”
The space is not only designed to support mental health, but is staffed for that purpose as well. Mental health professionals are a core part of the daily operations of the unit, assisting inmates and setting goals with them which in some cases have led to inmates being reintegrated into the general population, Rockvam said.
Rockvam also implemented a performance-based “Red, Yellow and Green Light” behavioral system, where inmates earn more liberties as they work with mental health staff. This sometimes includes receiving counseling and agreeing to take medications.
“As they come in, they’re restricted, but then as behavior improves, and they work with our staff, then at that point they can move up, and then to the point where they are on a green status,” Rockvam said. “And they have a lot more flexibility, they get out of their cells more, they get outside.”
Rockvam did not achieve this alone; he turned to other professionals for their input consistently along the way, he told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle.
One thing he said he heard consistently from psychologists and psychiatrists who had toured the pods was that inmates benefit from interacting with one another, even when they’re struggling with mental health issues.
Staff can also now call in one of the jail’s full-time master level mental health counselors to assist when inmates are in crisis, and have been trained on how to de-escalate those instances as well.
Another partner in this effort was the Wyoming Department of Health, which was able to assist the LCSO in getting inmates evaluated and on the necessary medications.
“We found that once we were able to get them on medications, they went from someone who was a threat and completely uncontrollable to somebody who now we can move into the general population,” Rockvam said.
That change was not only huge for inmates, but for the staff, Rockvam said. Working in the jail can be a high-stress job, Rockvam said, especially when inmates are violent, angry and threatening to kill staff.
“There were two primary reasons for us wanting to do this: one is to make it a better environment for the inmates that come in and have these issues, and then the other thing is to reduce the stress on our staff, because it was extremely stressful,” Rockvam said. “And I think we’ve been very successful in both.”
Not only have inmates made their way back to the general population, but some have also restored their mental health enough they no longer need a bed at the state hospital.
“Our goal is to stabilize,” Kozak said. “But we’ve actually restored people before they go to the state hospital so that they can stand trial, which is an added benefit we didn’t expect.”
The Special Management Housing Unit’s innovative approach has received national recognition outside of the award, recently being featured in Corrections1, a leading national law enforcement and corrections publication.
Locally, other county jails and their leadership have looked to LCSO to see if they, too can implement new ways to address inmate mental health, Rockvam said.
Rockvam said he was honored to be awarded the National Sheriffs’ Association Corrections/Jail Innovations of the Year Award.
“We’re just really, really proud of what we’re doing, and how we’re doing it,” Rockvam said.
